newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries steady at open, in range pre-FOMC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries steady at open, in range pre-FOMC.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities were nearly unchanged in early trade and the market seemed to be settling into a tight range before the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Tuesday, analysts said.
Despite generally friendly data in the last three days, the Street has no interest in chasing the market, they said.

"Retail has been off on the sidelines for three days or so, leaving a conglomeration of hedge funds, central banks and big dealers who want to punt this thing around, kicking the market up and down," said Doug Burtnick, at Technical Data.

Some reaction to April U.S. housing starts, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and the University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, could be expected, Burtnick, a senior fixed income analyst, said.
But after that, trade should dwindle.
"This is going to be a quick Friday," Burtnick said.
Housing starts were expected to have increased at an annualized rate of 1.43 million units, compared to 1.425 million units in March.
The preliminary Michigan consumer sentiment index for May is seen at 101.6, following April's final 101.4.
In early trade the 30-year bond was down 6/32 at 96-24/32, yielding 6.87 percent. The 10-year note was off 4/32 at 99-20/32 with a yield of 6.68.
Experts said they will continue to watch the currency markets, after bonds losely tracked the dollar's movements against the yen overnight. The dollar opened weaker near 115.40 yen.
But the main event comes on Tuesday, when Fed policy makers will decide whether or not to follow up their quarter-point fed funds increase in March with another adjustment.
The market is split on the prospects of another hike at on Tuesday, with futures and cash markets essentially pricing a 50/50 chance the Fed will go, analysts said.
"There will be a reaction if they go because the front end of the curve has to reprice," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securites.
"If they don't go, the big reaction might not be that they don't go but after the first big number, sort of saying whether or not they were right," he added.
Some buying was reported in the five-year note overnight.
The five-year was trading at 100-12/32, up 3/32, with a yield of 6.53 percent.
In the two-year note, analysts said the yield should hold above 6.2 percent before the meeting. It was up 1/32, at 100-08/32, yielding 6.23 percent.
In bills, the three-month was up five basis points at 5.03 percent. The six-month was up four basis points at 5.32 percent in early trade.
